content: The Every 15 Minutes program is a two-day initiative specifically designed for high school juniors and seniors. Its primary objective is to challenge these students to critically evaluate the consequences of drinking, driving, personal safety, and the importance of making responsible, mature decisions. The program not only addresses the dangers of alcohol-related crashes but also emphasizes the profound emotional and social impact such decisions can have on family and friends. History The Every 15 Minutes program originated in Canada and was later adopted in the United States, with its first implementation occurring in Spokane, Washington. The inaugural presentation of the program in Chico, California, was organized by the Chico Police Department in 1995. Planning and Events Planning The preparation for the Every 15 Minutes program begins several months before the actual event. This involves collaboration among all participating agencies, students, and school administrators. The planning process includes selecting the students who will actively participate in the program. First Day On the first day of the program, a student is removed from class at the very start of the school day. Subsequently, another student is removed every 15 minutes throughout the day. These students are not permitted to return to class until the following day. Instead, they spend 24 hours at a retreat alongside police officers and volunteers. During the day, a simulated traffic crash is staged on school grounds, involving some of the selected students. In this simulation, at least one student is portrayed as being killed. The staged crash is managed by local emergency response agencies, including police, fire, and medical services. A senior student plays the role of the drunk driver and is arrested by the local police. The entire scenario is enacted in front of the student body to replicate the real-life response to a drunk driving accident. After the crash scene, the removal of students from class every 15 minutes continues for the remainder of the day. Second Day The second day of the program features a school assembly where the participating students return. During the assembly, various community speakers address the audience, sharing perspectives on alcohol-related crashes. These presentations may include firsthand accounts of such incidents or insights from first responders. Additionally, the involved students and some of their parents share their experiences and reflections on the program. Questions Concerning Effectiveness Studies evaluating the Every 15 Minutes program have indicated that it may have a positive short-term impact on students' stated attitudes. However, there is no evidence to suggest that it leads to actual behavioral changes. This has drawn comparisons to the controversial D.A.R.E. anti-drug program, which has been criticized for creating the appearance of addressing a problem without achieving meaningful behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, questions have been raised about the program's foundational premise that one person dies every 15 minutes in an alcohol-related accident, as this statistic does not align with current data.
